components.plainExplanation: The Power LED shows that the Proxmark3 Easy is receiving power.
components.technicalExplanation: This LED is connected to the board power rail and is used as a simple visual power indicator.
components.pm3Use: Electron does not control this LED directly. It helps users confirm that USB power is present before running read-only checks.
components.safeNow: Check whether the LED is on after connecting USB. Do not use it as proof that the PM3 client is connected.
components.futureControlNotes: Future Device Studio could correlate the LED state with USB detection, but this would require either camera/user observation or firmware-reported state.
components.safetyNotes: Indicator only. No card or device data is changed.

components.plainExplanation: LED A is one of the activity indicators used by the Proxmark3 firmware.
components.technicalExplanation: The exact LED mapping depends on firmware and board variant. On Proxmark3 boards, LEDs are commonly used to show activity, modes or command progress.
components.pm3Use: Electron can later explain LED behavior during connection, scans or diagnostics if the firmware exposes reliable LED/status data.
components.safeNow: Observe LED behavior during read-only commands such as device information or scans.
components.futureControlNotes: A safe firmware-supported LED test command would let Device Studio identify LEDs one by one without changing RFID data.
components.safetyNotes: Observation is safe. Direct LED control should only be added later if the command is documented as diagnostic-only.

components.plainExplanation: LED B is an activity/status indicator.
components.technicalExplanation: This indicator may be driven by firmware for command, radio or standalone status depending on the PM3 build.
components.pm3Use: Later versions of Device Studio could show which PM3 state caused LED B to blink if firmware exposes the mapping.
components.safeNow: Use it as a visual hint only.
components.futureControlNotes: A read-only LED mapping report would be better than guessing from visual behavior.
components.safetyNotes: Do not infer card writes or security state from an LED alone.

components.plainExplanation: LED C is another board status indicator.
components.technicalExplanation: The firmware may use this LED for activity, radio state or standalone feedback.
components.pm3Use: Electron may later use it as part of a guided visual diagnostics workflow.
components.futureControlNotes: A firmware command such as a safe LED self-test would make this much easier to teach.
components.safetyNotes: Indicator only. This prototype does not control LEDs.

components.plainExplanation: LED D is part of the visible activity LED group.
components.technicalExplanation: Like the other activity LEDs, its exact behavior is firmware-dependent.
components.pm3Use: Future Device Studio versions could display LED role information from a device profile or firmware query.
components.safeNow: Use as a passive visual indicator.
components.futureControlNotes: Expose LED roles through firmware or a device profile instead of hardcoding assumptions.
components.safetyNotes: No direct control is implemented in Device Studio v1.

components.plainExplanation: The main USB port powers the Proxmark3 Easy and provides the connection to the computer.
components.technicalExplanation: The PM3 client communicates through the USB serial interface exposed by the device.
components.pm3Use: Electron uses this connection for Device Console, safe scans, hardware information and future read-only diagnostics.
components.safeNow: Connect the device with a reliable USB cable. If commands fail, check cable, port access and whether another app is using the serial port.
components.futureControlNotes: Device Studio can later show the detected serial path and active connection state here.
components.safetyNotes: Disconnecting during read-only commands is usually recoverable. Disconnecting during flashing would be risky, which is why flashing is out of scope.

components.plainExplanation: This side connector is visible on the Proxmark3 Easy enclosure view.
components.technicalExplanation: Exact function may vary by board/enclosure variant. Device Studio treats it as a visible connector until a device profile confirms its role.
components.pm3Use: Electron does not use this separately in v1.
components.safeNow: Use the main known USB connection for Electron unless the board documentation says otherwise.
components.futureControlNotes: A hardware profile could clarify connector roles for specific board revisions.
components.safetyNotes: Do not connect unknown accessories without checking the board documentation.

components.plainExplanation: The button is the physical user input on the PM3 board.
components.technicalExplanation: Firmware can read this button and use it for standalone functions or mode-specific behavior.
components.pm3Use: Electron may later explain when a workflow expects physical interaction, but Device Studio v1 does not map or control button behavior.
components.safeNow: Do not press the button during unknown standalone workflows unless Electron or the firmware documentation asks for it.
components.futureControlNotes: A read-only button-state command would allow Device Studio to show pressed/released state safely.
components.safetyNotes: Button behavior is firmware-dependent. Avoid using it as a hidden shortcut for risky workflows.

components.plainExplanation: The large PCB trace antenna is used for high-frequency RFID/NFC communication.
components.technicalExplanation: This antenna is designed for 13.56 MHz HF technologies such as ISO14443-A/B, MIFARE, DESFire, NTAG and ISO15693 depending on firmware support.
components.pm3Use: Electron uses HF through safe commands such as HF search and card information workflows.
components.safeNow: Place an HF card on the marked antenna area and use read-only scans.
components.futureControlNotes: Live tuning data from a read-only antenna tune command can help explain range and placement problems.
components.safetyNotes: Read-only HF identification is safe. Writing, emulation, restore and attack workflows are not part of Device Studio v1.

components.plainExplanation: The copper coil is the low-frequency antenna module, marked for 125 kHz on this asset.
components.technicalExplanation: LF antenna modules are used for low-frequency RFID families such as EM410x, HID Prox, Indala and T55xx-style tags depending on firmware and workflow.
components.pm3Use: Electron uses LF for safe identification such as LF search and future guided LF diagnostics.
components.safeNow: Place LF tags near the coil and run read-only LF identification only.
components.futureControlNotes: A clear LF antenna tune readout would help Device Studio explain weak coupling or poor tag placement.
components.safetyNotes: Read-only LF detection is safe. T55xx write/clone workflows are intentionally outside this prototype.

components.plainExplanation: The FPGA helps the PM3 handle timing-sensitive radio work.
components.technicalExplanation: The Xilinx Spartan device supports low-level signal processing tasks that need precise timing and are difficult to perform in normal application code alone.
components.pm3Use: Electron indirectly uses the FPGA whenever PM3 firmware performs RF operations that rely on low-level modulation or capture.
components.safeNow: Read hardware and firmware information only.
components.futureControlNotes: Device Studio would benefit from a read-only FPGA/status capability report.
components.safetyNotes: FPGA configuration is firmware-controlled. Do not expose FPGA reconfiguration or flashing in Device Studio v1.

components.plainExplanation: The MCU is the main controller that runs firmware and coordinates the board.
components.technicalExplanation: The AT91SAM7S512 controls USB communication, firmware flow and coordination with radio-related components.
components.pm3Use: Electron communicates with the firmware running on this controller through the PM3 client.
components.safeNow: Use read-only device information and status checks.
components.futureControlNotes: A richer firmware capability report would help Electron explain what this board can and cannot do.
components.safetyNotes: Firmware flashing affects this controller and can brick devices if interrupted. Flashing is deliberately not implemented here.

components.plainExplanation: These buffer chips help handle digital signal lines between board sections.
components.technicalExplanation: 74HC244 devices are octal buffers/line drivers used to isolate or drive digital signals.
components.pm3Use: Electron does not address these chips directly; they are part of the hardware path that makes RF and logic work reliable.
components.futureControlNotes: No direct user control should be needed. Hardware diagnostics could later report signal path health indirectly.
components.safetyNotes: Do not probe live hardware unless you know what you are doing; shorts or ESD can damage components.

components.plainExplanation: This area represents board memory/storage-related electronics that may be involved in firmware or persistent device state.
components.technicalExplanation: Exact part identification should be confirmed with board documentation or a schematic before Electron labels it as a specific flash chip.
components.pm3Use: Electron may later show firmware and storage-related status reported by read-only commands.
components.futureControlNotes: A board-revision profile should identify exact memory parts and whether firmware exposes any safe status.
components.safetyNotes: Do not add write, erase or flash features until a separate guarded Firmware Studio design exists.

components.plainExplanation: The power section conditions USB power for the board.
components.technicalExplanation: Regulators, filtering and related components help provide stable voltage rails to the MCU, FPGA and RF sections.
components.pm3Use: Electron may later show whether USB power and device communication look healthy based on read-only status.
components.safeNow: Use a good USB cable and avoid powering the board from unknown sources.
components.futureControlNotes: A read-only voltage/status report would be valuable if firmware exposes it.
components.safetyNotes: Hardware power faults can damage the board. Device Studio should explain symptoms but not attempt repair actions.
